title: Unless: Adding Excepto Que and Excepto Si

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *a menos que* "unless" from B1 Unit 21, and *a no ser que*, *salvo que* and *salvo si* from B2 Unit 9. Each one names the only thing that could stop the main clause from being true: *Iremos al parque a menos que llueva*. The exception has not happened yet, so these phrases take the subjunctive, with the same tense rule as in the last lesson. This lesson adds *excepto que* and *excepto si*, which work exactly like *salvo que* and *salvo si*. A useful test is to swap the phrase for *si no*: *Iremos a menos que llueva* means the same as *Iremos si no llueve*. The plan holds, and one exception could cancel it.

sections.title: Ways to say "unless"
rows: a menos que, a no ser que + subjunctive
unless, except if (a little more formal)
Iremos a menos que llueva. = Iremos si no llueve.
We will go unless it rains. = We will go if it does not rain.

items.spanish: El museo abre todos los días, excepto si hay una fiesta.
items.english: The museum opens every day, except if there is a festival.

items.spanish: Nadie entra a la sala excepto que tenga permiso.
items.english: No one enters the room unless they have permission.

items.spanish: No cambiaremos la fecha a menos que haya un imprevisto.
items.english: We will not change the date unless something unexpected happens.

items.spanish: Dijo que vendría a no ser que tuviera trabajo.
items.english: She said she would come unless she had work.

sections.content: Do not mix the two groups. Phrases with *que* (*a menos que*, *a no ser que*, *salvo que*, *excepto que*) take the subjunctive: *excepto que haya*. Phrases with *si* (*salvo si*, *excepto si*) take the indicative: *excepto si hay*. Do not use *aunque* here: *No saldremos aunque mejore el tiempo* means "We will not go out even if the weather improves", the opposite idea.
